description: We are Salvador and Leandro, final-year IT students at Universidad ORT Uruguay. In our capstone project we’re building a real-time rainfall visualizer for Uruguay’s meteorology institute (INUMET), working with weather data, interactive maps and full-stack web dev (React, Node.js, SQL Server, Azure). We want to use NASA Earth data on rainfall, soil moisture and water stress to build a practical web tool for agriculture. We work fast and aim to deliver a working prototype.
summary: RotaSat is a web app that helps farmers in Uruguay choose crop rotations that protect their soil and stand up to a changing climate. A farmer clicks on their field on a map, sets their priorities (production, soil health, water saving) and picks a climate scenario. RotaSat then fetches NASA Earth observation data for that exact location and ranks four typical Uruguayan rotations, with five transparent scores and plain-language warnings. Its stress test replays the real 2022–23 drought, one of the worst in Uruguay's recent history, showing which rotations hold up and which are most vulnerable. This matters because rotation choices last for years, and farmers rarely have a simple way to test them against their own field's climate, soil and goals.
details:
What it does

RotaSat compares four crop rotations that are common in Uruguay: continuous soybean, wheat / second soybean, wheat-soybean followed by cover crop-maize, and a crop-pasture system (3 years of crops + 3 years of perennial pasture). For any field in Uruguay it returns a ranking with a 0–100 score on five criteria: soil health, erosion control, water balance, climate resilience and production. Each rotation also gets explainable warnings, such as "At least one day ≥37 °C during soybean flowering in 60% of years".

How it works

1. The farmer selects a field on the map (or tries an example field) and sets three priority sliders.

2. The backend fetches, for that point: 20 years of monthly climate and root-zone soil moisture from NASA POWER, terrain slope from NASA SRTM, and soil texture and organic carbon from ISRIC SoilGrids.

3. A transparent scoring engine evaluates each rotation:

- Soil health: months of ground cover, crop residue, share of grasses and presence of perennial pasture.

- Erosion control: a simplified RUSLE-inspired index (rainfall × slope × soil erodibility × bare-soil factor).

- Water balance: seasonal rainfall and root-zone soil moisture vs. each crop's water needs (FAO-56).

- Climate resilience: frequency of extreme heat during flowering and frost for sensitive crops.

- Production: grain harvests per year, adjusted by water availability.

4. The final score weights these criteria using the farmer's priorities.

5. Climate scenarios: normal years (2005–2024 average), the driest year on record (typically the 2023 drought) and the hottest year on record. In stress scenarios each rotation shows its score drop versus normal years.

Benefits

- Turns complex satellite data into a simple, visual decision tool for farmers, agronomists and students.

- Every number is explainable; there is no black box.

- Shows the real trade-offs: in the 2023 drought, diversified rotations stay on top while continuous soybean ranks last.

What we hope to achieve

Help Uruguayan farmers make more resilient long-term decisions and support the country's mandatory Soil Use and Management Plans. Next steps: add NASA SMAP soil moisture and GPM IMERG rainfall, integrate official Uruguayan soil maps (MGAP), and allow custom rotations with economic data.

Tools and technologies

React + Vite and Leaflet (frontend, deployed on Vercel), Node.js + Express (backend, deployed on Render), NASA POWER API, OpenTopoData (SRTM), ISRIC SoilGrids API, GitHub.

Source code and documentation: https://github.com/salvaespiga/field-shift-uy

Limitations

RotaSat is an exploration tool, not an agronomic prescription. It uses monthly data and simplified, indicative crop parameters, and version 1 is limited to Uruguay.
